title: Healthcare waste segregation
blurb: The HTM 07-01 colour code, which dental waste goes where, handling bags and sharps bins safely, and the paperwork that proves lawful disposal.
question: After a surgical extraction you clear the surgery. You have blood-soaked gauze, a used local anaesthetic cartridge, the extracted tooth (which has an amalgam filling), the clean wrapper from the suture pack and the patient's used bib. Where does each item go?

teach.h: Why waste is sorted at source
teach.body: Segregation means putting each item into the right colour-coded container at the point where it's created. It keeps staff, waste carriers and the public safe, keeps the practice within the law, and controls cost: infectious waste is far more expensive to treat than domestic waste, so domestic rubbish in a clinical bag wastes money, and clinical waste in a domestic bin is dangerous and illegal. Clear labels help new and temporary staff. If you're unsure where something goes, ask or check the policy.

items.label: Orange
items.sub: Known infectious waste for alternative treatment, e.g. blood-soaked swabs and dressings

items.label: Yellow
items.sub: Infectious waste for incineration, including waste contaminated with medicines

items.label: Yellow and black ('tiger')
items.sub: Offensive or hygiene waste: not infectious, e.g. bibs, couch roll, non-infectious PPE. Never sharps

items.label: White
items.sub: Dental amalgam, in a container with mercury vapour suppressant

items.label: Red
items.sub: Anatomical waste, in rigid red or red-lidded containers

items.label: Black
items.sub: Domestic waste, e.g. food, clean paper towels

teach.caption: Gypsum (plaster models) also goes in its own specifically marked bin, with infectious gypsum kept separate. Clean recyclables go in clear or white recycling sacks. Scotland and Northern Ireland use their own colour systems.

items.label: Yellow lid
items.sub: Sharps contaminated with medicines, e.g. used LA cartridges and needles

items.label: Orange lid
items.sub: Used sharps NOT contaminated with medicines

items.label: Purple lid
items.sub: Sharps contaminated with cytotoxic or cytostatic medicines

teach.caption: The lid colour tells you the stream. Most dental sharps (LA needles and cartridges) are medicinally contaminated, so they go in the yellow-lidded bin.

teach.caption: Teeth without amalgam may be treated as infectious waste. HTM 07-01 says broken or jagged teeth often go in the yellow-lidded sharps bin, and whole non-infectious teeth can be offensive waste. Follow your practice policy.

teach.body: Dental amalgam contains mercury, so it is hazardous waste with its own code. It never goes in domestic, clinical or offensive bags. Amalgam capsules, waste amalgam and suction trap contents go in a marked white container with mercury vapour suppressant, which stops toxic vapour escaping. Teeth with amalgam fillings go into amalgam waste, and infectious amalgam waste goes in its own separate container. Spilled mercury is dealt with using a spillage kit (see the spillages lesson).

items: Fill bags only to the marked fill line, so they can be sealed safely and won't split.
Seal securely and label or tag the bag so it can be traced back to the practice.
Never press waste down by hand: hidden sharps cause injuries.
Wear suitable PPE, carry bags by the neck away from your body or use a trolley, then perform hand hygiene.
If a bag leaks, place it in a second suitable bag and report it. If it tears, contain the spill and follow the spillage procedure.
Store sealed bags in a secure, locked area until collection: never in escape routes, public areas or next to sterile packs.

teach.h: Duty of care and consignment notes
teach.body: Duty of care means everyone who produces waste must make sure it's managed properly from production to final disposal. The practice is the producer: it must use an authorised (licensed) carrier and keep accurate paperwork. Hazardous waste, such as infectious or amalgam waste, needs a hazardous waste consignment note when collected; the producer is legally responsible for its accuracy. Non-hazardous waste moves on a waste transfer note. HTM 07-01's checklist says keep both for at least two years; hazardous waste rules in England set three years for consignment records, so follow your practice policy.

teach.caption: Each note describes the waste in words, gives its European Waste Catalogue (EWC) code and states the quantity.

teach.text: Tiger (yellow and black) means OFFENSIVE waste: unpleasant but not infectious, and it must never contain sharps. Blood-soaked swabs and dressings go in orange infectious waste, and LA cartridges go in the yellow-lidded sharps bin, not the orange-lidded one.

items: Orange: infectious. Yellow: infectious for incineration or medicine-contaminated. Tiger: offensive.
Purple: cytotoxic. Blue: medicines. White: amalgam. Red: anatomical. Black: domestic.
Sharps lids: yellow (medicines, e.g. LA cartridges), orange (no medicines), purple (cytotoxic).
Fill to the line, seal, label, never compact by hand, store securely.
Hazardous waste needs a consignment note; keep notes at least 2 years (HTM 07-01).

summary: You can now explain why waste is segregated, use the HTM 07-01 colour code for bags, bins and sharps lids, place common dental waste (including amalgam) in the right stream, handle and store waste bags safely, and describe the duty of care paperwork that proves lawful disposal.

A.q: A dental nurse finds blood-soaked gauze in the domestic waste bin. What is the best action?
options: Leave it, as the amount is small
Move it to the infectious waste stream
Put it in the recycling instead
Pour disinfectant into the domestic bin
A.why: Blood-soaked swabs and gauze are infectious clinical waste and must go into the correct infectious stream, not domestic waste.

whyNot.0: Quantity doesn't change the waste category.
whyNot.2: Contaminated items must never go into recycling.
whyNot.3: Disinfecting the bin doesn't make clinical waste legal to dispose of as domestic.

A.q: Which container should a used local anaesthetic cartridge go into?
options: A yellow and black offensive bag
A.why: LA cartridges are medicinally contaminated sharps, which go in a yellow-lidded sharps bin.

whyNot.0: Orange lids are for sharps not contaminated with medicines.
whyNot.1: Offensive bags must never contain sharps.
whyNot.3: White containers are for amalgam waste.

A.q: Which waste stream is identified by yellow and black ('tiger') striped bags?
A.why: Tiger bags hold offensive or hygiene waste: non-infectious but unpleasant items such as bibs and couch roll.

whyNot.0: Known infectious waste goes in orange (or yellow) containers.
whyNot.2: Amalgam goes in a white container with mercury suppressant.

B.q: An extracted tooth contains an amalgam filling. Where should it go?
B.why: HTM 07-01 says teeth with amalgam fillings go into amalgam waste, because of their mercury content.

whyNot.1: Teeth are never domestic waste, and amalgam is hazardous.
whyNot.2: Offensive waste isn't suitable for mercury-containing items.
whyNot.3: Blue bins are for medicines, not amalgam.

B.q: A clinical waste bag is filled well past its marked line. Why is this a problem?
options: It changes the colour of the bag
It may split or not seal safely
It makes the bag too light to lift
It turns the waste into domestic waste
B.why: Overfilled bags can split and can't be sealed properly, risking spillage and injury.

whyNot.0: Filling doesn't change the bag colour.
whyNot.2: An overfilled bag is heavier, not lighter.
whyNot.3: The waste category doesn't change with the fill level.

B.q: A hazardous waste collection takes place. Who is legally responsible for the accuracy of the consignment note?
B.why: HTM 07-01 says the producer is legally responsible for ensuring the accuracy of a consignment note.

whyNot.0: The carrier signs too, but the producer is responsible for accuracy.
whyNot.1: The council doesn't complete the practice's consignment notes.
whyNot.3: The Environment Agency regulates; it doesn't complete the note.

C.q: Out-of-date, non-cytotoxic medicines need disposing of. Which container is correct?
C.why: HTM 07-01 uses blue-lidded containers for non-cytotoxic medicinal waste.

whyNot.0: Purple is for cytotoxic and cytostatic waste.
whyNot.2: Medicines must never go in domestic waste.

C.q: Full clinical waste bags are waiting for collection. Where should they be kept?
options: In the corridor by the fire exit
C.why: Waste must be stored securely, away from the public, escape routes and clean areas, until the licensed carrier collects it.

whyNot.1: Bags must never obstruct escape routes.
whyNot.2: Waste must be kept away from clean, sterilised stock.
whyNot.3: Public areas risk access and tampering.

C.q: Which item can go in the domestic or recycling waste?
options: Clean card from a sealed box
C.why: Clean, uncontaminated paper and card packaging can go in domestic or recycling waste.

whyNot.0: Used clinical gloves belong in the clinical or offensive stream, per policy.
whyNot.2: Blood-stained items are infectious clinical waste.
whyNot.3: Amalgam waste goes in the white amalgam container.

reteach.title: Think of household recycling, with higher stakes
reteach.question: At home you sort glass, paper and food into different bins. What changes when the 'rubbish' could carry infection or mercury?

blocks.body: At home, the wrong item in the recycling might just get a sticker on your bin. In a dental practice, the wrong item in the wrong bag can injure a waste handler, spread infection, release mercury, or break the law. So the colours do the thinking for everyone down the line: orange says 'infectious', tiger says 'unpleasant but not infectious', white says 'amalgam', and a sharps bin's lid says what's on the needles. Sorting at the point of use means nobody has to sort it later.

blocks.text: Domestic waste in a clinical bag isn't 'playing it safe': it raises disposal costs and is poor segregation.

explain.body: Orange: infectious for treatment. Yellow: infectious for incineration or medicine-contaminated. Tiger: offensive. Purple: cytotoxic. Blue: medicines. White: amalgam. Red: anatomical. Black: domestic.

test.q: Which colour identifies cytotoxic and cytostatic waste?
test.why: HTM 07-01 uses purple for cytotoxic and cytostatic waste.

whyNot.3: White is for dental amalgam (and marked gypsum bins).

explain.body: Yellow lid: sharps contaminated with medicines (LA cartridges and needles). Orange lid: sharps without medicines. Purple lid: cytotoxic sharps.

test.q: A used needle that was never in contact with any medicine needs disposing of. Which sharps bin lid colour is correct?
test.why: Orange-lidded sharps bins are for used sharps not contaminated with medicines.

whyNot.0: Yellow lids are for medicinally contaminated sharps.
whyNot.2: Purple lids are for cytotoxic sharps.
whyNot.3: Blue lids are for medicines, not sharps.

explain.body: Fill to the line, seal, label, never compact by hand. Leaking bag: double-bag and report. Store in a secure, locked area away from exits, the public and sterile stock.

test.q: A clinical waste bag is found leaking fluid. What is the best response?
options: Tape over the leak and carry on
Place it in a second bag and report it
Empty it into a new bag by hand, wearing gloves
Leave it for the waste carrier
test.why: A leaking bag is placed safely into a second suitable bag and the incident reported.

whyNot.0: Tape won't reliably contain the leak.
whyNot.2: Handling the contents risks sharps injury and contamination.
whyNot.3: Leaving it risks spillage and exposure.

explain.body: Duty of care: the producer makes sure waste is handled by authorised carriers from production to disposal. Hazardous waste: consignment note. Non-hazardous: waste transfer note. Keep at least two years (HTM 07-01).

test.q: Why should waste collections be documented?
options: To record lawful transfer and disposal
To work out staff holiday cover
test.why: Consignment and transfer notes are the legal record that waste was transferred to an authorised carrier and disposed of properly.

whyNot.1: Holiday cover has nothing to do with waste records.
whyNot.3: Sterilizer records are kept in the sterilizer logbook.
